analysis.one_liner: Repeals an export tax subsidy ruled illegal, replacing it with a sweeping corporate tax cut and some worker protections.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 92-5 on May 11, 2004, but the bill never became law; the House instead took up its own companion bill, H.R. 4520, which became the year's corporate tax law.
analysis.plain_summary: The World Trade Organization ruled that a US tax break for export income was an illegal export subsidy, and Europe began adding tariffs on American exports in response. This bill repealed that export subsidy and, to win votes, replaced it with a deduction worth up to 9 percent of income from domestic manufacturing and production, plus a long list of tax breaks for multinationals, oil and gas producers, timber owners, filmmakers, and energy companies. It also carried provisions unrelated to exports: new penalties and disclosure rules for corporate tax shelters, IRS whistleblower awards, limits on outsourcing federal and state work overseas, and a block on the administration's new overtime rules that would have cut overtime pay for workers earning under about $23,660 a year. The Senate passed it 92-5, but the House wrote its own version instead, and that companion bill — not this one — became law.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had become law, the largest winners were domestic manufacturers and multinational corporations: the new deduction for domestic production income, extended foreign tax credit carryforwards, relaxed rules for controlled foreign corporations, and a 5.25 percent rate on certain repatriated dividends. Oil and gas producers, timber owners, filmmakers, ethanol and renewable energy companies, and utilities gained targeted credits and depreciation rules. Workers also benefited in specific ways: the bill blocked the administration's overtime rules that would have removed overtime pay for employees earning under $23,660, restricted sending federal and state work overseas, and created IRS whistleblower awards. Tax enforcement benefited from funding and new penalties against shelter promoters.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a deduction of up to 9 percent of income from domestic production activities — manufacturing, construction, farming, and certain engineering and architectural work — phased in through 2009, and limited to 50 percent of the employer's W-2 wages, so the benefit is tied to paying workers in the United States.

Prohibits the Department of Labor from issuing overtime rules that exempt any employee earning less than $23,660 a year from overtime pay, and invalidates the overtime regulations the administration issued in April 2004.

Bars outsourced federal contract work from being performed overseas, restricts federal funds from being spent by states on work performed abroad, and requires federal agencies to report purchases of foreign-made goods.

Cracks down on corporate tax shelters: it codifies the economic-substance doctrine, imposes penalties up to 40 percent on understatements from tax-avoidance transactions, forces advisors to disclose shelter deals, and funds IRS enforcement against offshore evasion.
Establishes awards of 10 to 30 percent for IRS whistleblowers who report large-scale tax evasion and creates a Whistleblower Office to process their claims.

Includes several provisions of direct public benefit: tax-exempt bonds for green building projects, a Medicaid option covering sickle cell disease treatment, deduction of attorney fees in discrimination cases, and exclusion of National Health Service Corps loan repayments from income.

analysis.who_pays: The cost of the corporate tax cuts and energy credits falls on the Treasury, meaning other taxpayers or federal borrowing, since the bill replaces one export subsidy with a larger set of deductions and credits partly offset by shelter penalties and enforcement. Corporations using aggressive tax shelters and companies that had moved headquarters offshore to cut taxes would bear new penalties and anti-inversion rules. The Treasury and IRS gained responsibilities but also gained user-fee authority and private collection contracts to offset costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, through lost Treasury revenue

drawbacks.text: Beyond the WTO-mandated export-subsidy repeal, the bill layers on narrowly targeted tax breaks for specific industries — 7-year depreciation for motorsports entertainment complexes, modified taxation of imported archery products, capital gains treatment for outright timber sales, a 12-month holding period for horses — that serve particular businesses rather than any broad public purpose.

The energy title grants a long list of tax credits and faster depreciation to oil and gas producers, including a credit for oil and gas from marginal wells, expensing of costs to comply with EPA sulfur regulations, and a credit for Alaska natural gas, adding to the bill's cost to the Treasury.

The anti-outsourcing title only takes effect 30 days after the Secretary of Commerce certifies it will not result in the loss of more jobs than it will protect, and it exempts defense, homeland security, intelligence, and all procurement covered by the WTO Government Procurement Agreement — greatly narrowing what it actually restrains.

The bill is sprawling: replacing one export subsidy opens the door to hundreds of provisions across international tax, energy, housing, and agriculture, and the added complexity and revenue cost fall on ordinary taxpayers either through higher future taxes or added debt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill honestly did what it was written to do: it removed an illegal export subsidy that was costing American exporters escalating EU tariffs, and it contained the strongest corporate tax-shelter crackdown and enforcement funding in years, plus real overtime and anti-outsourcing protections for workers. But it carried that necessary fix wrapped in a sprawling set of industry-specific tax breaks — special depreciation for racetracks, tax relief for archery imports, capital gains treatment for timber and horses — of the kind that erode the tax base and shift costs to everyone else. And the worker protections were the most expendable part: they survived in the Senate bill but did not survive the legislative process that produced the final law. The good provisions did not justify the giveaway breadth, and the worker provisions did not endure.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the bill 92-5, but the House never voted on it; instead the House worked from its own companion bill, H.R. 4520, which became the 2004 corporate tax law, and this Senate bill simply expired with the Congress.

narrative.text: After two failed recommittal fights, the Senate broke a filibuster threat by invoking cloture 90-8 and then passed the bill 92-5 on May 11, 2004, with 44 of 48 Democrats and 47 of 51 Republicans voting yes.
The bill's last recorded action, on July 15, 2004, notes its companion measure in the House, H.R. 4520 — the vehicle that carried the corporate tax package to enactment.
No further action was taken on S. 1637 itself; the Congress ended on January 3, 2005 without the Senate bill ever receiving a House vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations, manufacturers, and energy, timber, and film interests came out ahead: the corporate tax package was enacted anyway through the House companion bill, while the Senate version's overtime-pay protections and outsourcing restrictions were the parts that did not survive into the final law.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: Senator from Iowa; Chair, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, guided it through the Finance Committee (reported twice, including after a recommittal with instructions), and managed it to Senate passage, 92-5.

for.name: Bill Frist
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor and moved twice to recommit it to the Finance Committee with an amendment; after cloture on the recommittal failed twice (51-47 and 50-47), the recommitted version was reported back and the bill passed.

for.name: European Union
for.role: Trading partner of the United States
for.what_they_did: Began imposing escalating retaliatory tariffs on American exports after the World Trade Organization ruled the export subsidy illegal, creating pressure on Congress to pass a fix.

against.name: 45 of 48 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted nearly unanimously (1 yea, 45 nay) against cutting off debate on the first motion to recommit the bill to the Finance Committee, blocking the recommittal.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's restrictions on the administration's new overtime-pay regulations; the overtime protections did not appear in the law that was ultimately enacted from the House companion bill.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was overwhelmingly bipartisan (92-5, with 44 of 48 Democrats and 47 of 51 Republicans in favor), though the floor fights over recommittal split by party, with 45 of 48 Democrats blocking cloture on Leader Frist's recommittal motions while 47-50 Republicans supported it.

industries.note: The bill loosens the international tax rules: it extends the foreign tax credit carryforward to 20 years, repeals the 90-percent limit on the alternative minimum tax foreign tax credit, relaxes subpart F rules for controlled foreign corporations, and taxes certain repatriated dividends at 5.25 percent. These changes cut the tax bills of companies with large overseas operations.

The 9 percent deduction for domestic production income — capped at 50 percent of W-2 wages — is the bill's centerpiece replacement for the export subsidy, and it lowers taxes for companies producing in the United States.

The energy title provides a credit for production from marginal wells, expensing of EPA sulfur-compliance costs, faster depreciation for natural gas pipelines, and a credit for Alaska natural gas, on top of extended percentage-depletion relief.

Timber sales qualify for capital gains treatment, reforestation costs can be expensed, and timber REIT safe harbors are loosened, converting ordinary income into lower-taxed gains for a concentrated landowning interest.
Producers may expense up to $15-20 million of production costs in the year incurred, a substantial cash-flow benefit for studios.

The bill imposes disclosure requirements, daily penalties of $10,000, penalties up to 40 percent on transactions lacking economic substance, and injunction authority against advisors who market abusive shelters.

industries.industry: Companies that inverted offshore and wealthy expatriates
industries.note: Inverted corporations are treated as domestic for tax purposes, insiders face a 20 percent excise tax on stock compensation around an inversion, and wealthy citizens who renounce citizenship face a tax on unrealized gains as if sold the day before expatriating.

The bill creates the volumetric ethanol excise tax credit, a biodiesel credit, extends the renewable electricity production credit to more resources, and adds credits for hybrid and alternative-fuel vehicles and energy-efficient homes.
